Comes across to me as a sort of 'race' condition in your code. As in, the character is being duplicated while it is also being freed. This could also explain the corruption, as the duplication might then reference stale or corrupted data. One possible workaround in your code would be to add a boolean which you toggle before and after duplication.

To then add a check on the code that calls the free. Only freeing it when it is not being duplicated. So the two processes, the duplication and the freeing do not accidentally get called simultaneously.

The duplicate is not freed early. Note that in the above images, the transition animation (ellipse expanding, fading between two scenes) is still playing- the duplicate will not be freed until after the entire animation finishes via the tween.

I just placed a breakpoint on the `duplicate()` call. The errors here occur DURING the duplicate call itself, as they appear when I step over just that one line, with the `queue_free` on the duplicate not having any chance to run yet.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/2e024f07-1c0b-42d4-8c16-13b2006878bc)

Also, to be clear, the ORIGINAL character is not being freed whatsoever as part of this transition.

I didn't mean it as an insult of your code, or anything like that. I simply have no access to the code. So, couldn't be sure you weren't pushing the engine to its breaking point. I've done that myself.

Anyhow, thanks for the additional information. Something peculiar does indeed seem to be going on.

From the error message this looks like a duplicate of #96246, in this case the error only appears when duplicating a node with internal child nodes (the internal nodes wasn't being duplicated and raise the child count difference error).

The talk in this old PR is also relevant: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/96018, also for me, it happens with `MeshInstance3D` objects, so not necessarily internal nodes.

I narrowed down the problem a bit and it seems that duplicating nodes (usually PackedScenes) with dynamically created children that's also oddly in some deep hierarchy (Like Root/Node/SubNode) breaks.

What's extra odd is when SubNode is a `Node3D`, it works, when it's a `Skeleton3D`, it breaks.

Although I don't recommend this intrusive way of managing nodes. Since you have already added a node using the script, why can't you add a node again using the script?  

I think a sub-scene should be **self-managed** and behave like a class object, with the nodes inside it best considered private to the scene root. You can indirectly change its node structure externally using variables or methods of the scene root.

It's not that you can't break a sub-scene, but the script that breaks it will/should be responsible for it.

> I think a sub-scene should be **self-managed** and behave like a class object, with the nodes inside it best considered private to the scene root. You can indirectly change its node structure externally using variables or methods of the scene root.

@Rindbee :

> Since you have already added a node using the script, why can't you add a node again using the script?

That would be part of what `duplicate()` is for, no? A script is calling that to create a full copy, including changes- if it wanted a copy without changes it would call `.instantiate()` on the PackedScene.

> It's not that you can't break a sub-scene, but the script that breaks it will/should be responsible for it.

The script breaking it, is the engine itself, inside the `duplicate()` function, by not properly duplicating.

This is because the copying of properties does not follow the same principles as when copying nodes. This is a bug. So is the number of nodes as expected? 

This situation is exactly why I feel that nodes added by the script should not be copied. It is more common.

> here's the thing, if you can't duplicate a scene with the changes you made with a command called duplicate where everyone expects it to do what it's supposed to, what's the point of having duplicate at all then?

You can set the owner, although I feel like this is probably mostly used by plugins. 

If you want the nodes to behave the same as in the editor or a little more flexibly, you can set the owner and make sure the code that adds and removes nodes doesn't run often.

If you want to be more casual, I don't think your intentions are easy to predict.


> That would be part of what `duplicate()` is for, no? A script is calling that to create a full copy, including changes- if it wanted a copy without changes it would call `.instantiate()` on the PackedScene.
 


I don't think so, because users are creative. So it's hard to predict the exact behavior and intention of user scripts.

However, the behavior in the editor should be a demonstration of predictable behavior. 

If you want nodes added by the script to behave the same as they do in the editor, you should configure them the same way.


The engine provides two common ways:
1. Use internal nodes and expose properties, and change the behavior of internal nodes through properties. For example, nodes such as ScrollContainer. This may require writing self-management code.
2. Use Scene and mark it as managed by the engine by setting the owner.  This is more free than the first way, and the editor does extra work.

What's more freeing is scripting, which is less predictable behavior. But if your script follows the above two ways, the engine may be able to help.

@Rindbee, after thinking more on your comments, I understand how you might want to `duplicate()` while excluding dynamically added nodes. #84824 broke compatibility without stating it, so the change in default behavior was being treated as a regression. I suggest that we instead consider making this behavior optional by the user's choice. Since this issue itself is fixed, I propose we continue this discussion as a proposal to add optional functionality of ignoring script-added children when duplicating via instancing: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11942

You can test the project again, I'm not sure what you want, but now you get two new nodes each time you call `duplicate()`, one dynamically added by the script of the duplicated node at `_ready()`, and one added by `duplicate()`.

In a complex scene, if the parent scene always has to consider the node management in the child scene, it may be a headache. So a simple management principle is to make the sub-scene behave like a single node.

> In a complex scene, if the parent scene always has to consider the node management in the child scene, it may be a headache. So a simple management principle is to make the sub-scene behave like a single node.

...if you duplicate a single node, you're duplicating it including it's changes. Is duplicating it but NOT some of it's changes (notably child nodes) not doing the opposite of "making the sub-scene behave like a single node"?

The child nodes of the scene root of the sub-scene have different owners for those added in the sub-scene and those added in the parent scene. This is the key to distinguishing them.

If you need to build and configure a single node that is more complex, why not build a prototype using a scene or a global script class?

@Rindbee here's the thing, you're kinda blaming a rookie coding problem on a method that should do as the name implies, `_duplicate()`.
Because if you're going to consider all fail safe situations not to make duplicate actually duplicate whatever is inside, we should also consider recursivity, null pointer access, cyclic inclusion and so on, because duplication may or may not duplicate dynamic nodes, but it duplicates script and node properties which may as well fail due to rookie coding mistakes.

At the end of the day, we already have `instantiate()` to create a clean object that has nothing of the problems anyone could possibly have.

-------
A real world example of this is my project, where I do runtime baking of character textures, portrait image and stitch meshes, to prevent the game from freezing, I duplicate the current character object and run the entire process on a thread, the character contains some meshes like weapons or armor added dynamically when needed, duplicating used to work fine before 4.2, after that I had to replace that to `instantiate()`, copy some properties from one to another and update the entire character customization just to make the clone match the original, all that only for baking and then deleting.


I won't stretch this anymore as the fix has already been merged and there's a proposal for more discussion, just dropping my last 2 cents to say this is a very needed method behavior, just like any other game engines out there with their own version of "deep copying" nodes: https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Object.Instantiate.html

> duplicating used to work fine before 4.2, after that I had to replace that to `instantiate()`, 

After setting the owner for dynamically added nodes, `duplicate(7)` will still work. Of course, I forgot to document this. Sorry for that. I think setting owner will make `duplicate()` more flexible. Owner can be seen as a flag that lets `duplicate(7)` skip or not skip..

```gdscript
extends Node

func _ready() -> void:
	var n = Node.new()
	get_child(0).add_child(n)
	n.owner = get_tree().get_root()
	
```
